title: Black Forest Trifle
subtitle: Chocolate sponge, dark berries, sherry custard, and dark chocolate cream
excerpt: The flavours of Black Forest gateau in trifle form, sherry-soaked sponge, blackberries, a dark chocolate custard, and cream dusted with cocoa.
sourceNotes: A British riff on the German Schwarzwälder Kirschtorte, recast as a trifle. The layered format and sherry-soaked sponge base are classic British trifle traditions; the chocolate custard and dark berry combination evoke the gateau's characteristic flavours.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The sponge, fruit, and custard layers can be assembled up to a day ahead. Add the cream and chocolate shavings on the day of serving.

content.text: Black Forest trifle takes the flavours of the German gateau, chocolate, dark fruit, and cream, and layers them into the British trifle format. The custard is enriched with melted dark chocolate, giving it a deep, glossy finish and a bitter edge that cuts through the sweet cream on top. A chocolate custard needs a little more attention than a plain one; the chocolate can seize if the heat is too high, so keep the temperature gentle throughout.

Spread the sponge fingers with raspberry jam and arrange them in a single layer across the base of a large glass dish. Pour the sweet sherry evenly over the sponge and leave to soak for 10 minutes. Scatter the blackberries over the soaked sponge.

Melt the dark chocolate in a heatproof bowl set over a pan of barely simmering water, stirring occasionally. Set aside. In a separate bowl, whisk the egg yolks, caster sugar, and cornflour together until smooth. Heat the milk in a medium saucepan until steaming. Pour the hot milk into the egg mixture in a slow stream, whisking constantly, then return to the saucepan over a low heat. Stir continuously for 8 to 10 minutes until the custard thickens. Remove from the heat and whisk in the melted chocolate until fully combined. Pour through a sieve over the blackberry layer, press cling film onto the surface, and cool to room temperature.

Refrigerate for at least 4 hours until the custard layer is fully set. Whip the double cream with the icing sugar to soft peaks and spoon over the custard. Dust generously with cocoa powder before serving.

items.symptom: Chocolate custard is grainy or split
items.cause: The chocolate was added when the custard was too hot, or the heat was too high during cooking.
items.fix: Let the custard cool for 2 minutes off the heat before whisking in the chocolate. If the custard looks split, blend briefly with a stick blender.

items.symptom: Blackberries are very sharp against the chocolate
items.cause: The berries are naturally tart, which contrasts strongly with sweet chocolate custard.
items.fix: Toss the blackberries with 1 tablespoon of caster sugar and leave for 10 minutes before layering.

items.symptom: Custard layer is too thick to pour
items.cause: The custard cooked for too long or cooled too much before pouring.
items.fix: Pour the custard while it is still warm and fluid. If it has set, warm gently in the saucepan over a very low heat, stirring, until it loosens.

content.text: Keeps covered in the fridge for up to 2 days. Add the cocoa dusting on the day of serving.
